Go.

For most real-world work — services, APIs, CLI tools, internal tooling — Go ships faster, reads cleaner six months later, and onboards new teammates without a week of borrow-checker archaeology. The concurrency model is genuinely good, the standard library covers most of what you need, and the compilation speed keeps iteration tight.

Rust is the right call when you're writing a runtime, an OS component, something embedded, or anything where a GC pause or a byte of wasted memory is unacceptable. If that describes your project, Rust isn't even a tradeoff — it's just correct. But that's a narrower category than its hype implies.

For the remaining 80% of software, Go's simplicity is a feature, not a limitation.
